summary.text:
A quiet, well-reconciled treasury report. The Cabinet on 30 June 2026 was asked to NOTE the outturn. Our loan-level PWLB file matches the paper's own PWLB total to within £14k on £115.6m — we hold all 51 of their PWLB loans at a weighted 3.7329% against their reported 3.74% on total debt. The balance-sheet identity CFR − external borrowing − OLTL = internal borrowing holds exactly at £20.586m.

The most interesting number is a rise, not a level: the HRA financing-cost ratio has gone from 15.4% to 18.1%, driven by more capital borrowing and lower-than-forecast dwelling rents. HRA is already 77% of their CFR. The paper also discloses a concrete refi pressure — the £7.4m at 2.92% that matured on 28 March 2026 (part of the £66.4m Housing Finance Reforms tranche drawn on 28 March 2012) was replaced along with others at 4.15%, adding £190k per annum to the interest bill.

Nine new PWLB draws of £22.0m in Oct 2025 – Feb 2026 came in at 4.02–4.28% for 3–8 year money — well below the year-end certainty EIP rates the paper itself prints (5.26–5.52% for 1–10y at 31-Mar-26). The 2025/26 term-out looks well-timed against the March 2026 curve.

The S151 is referenced only by title ("Interim Deputy Chief Executive and Section 151 Officer") in this paper and in the earlier strategy (3 February 2026). No name printed. No officer address published. That is why this note is drafted but blocked on the recipient line.

status.note: Paper names no S151 officer and prints no contact address. Draft is written and machine-checked. Next likely treasury item to Cabinet is the mid-year update in autumn 2026, then the 2026/27 strategy through Cabinet early Feb 2027 — neither date printed in the paper.

officer.subject: 51 loans matching to £14k — and the 2012 tranche now starts to roll
officer.body:
Hi,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, and every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on the annual outturn Cabinet noted on 30 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The report is clear and well laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

As a cross-check that our numbers tie to yours: we hold 51 PWLB loans for Broxtowe totalling £115,571,971 at a weighted 3.7329%. The paper's Appendix 1 sums to £115.558m of PWLB (long-term £101.239m plus the PWLB portions of the short-term line — £7.9m maturity, £6.4m EIP, £19k annuity). That's a match to £14k. You can see our loan-level file at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

The balance-sheet identity ties too: CFR £139.158m less external borrowing £118.572m less zero other long-term liabilities is £20.586m, which is exactly the Over/(Under) Borrowing line on page 11 of your Appendix 2.

The number that most caught our eye is one you disclose yourself. On page 6 you say the £7.4m at 2.92% that matured in March, together with other loans, was replaced at 4.15% and that this adds around £190k per annum. That's the first slice of the £66.4m Housing Finance Reform tranche from 28 March 2012, and the paper reminds the reader that those preferential rates still hold the average rate down. What's on your file with us that dates from that window and could roll behind it we can see loan by loan.

And a second one, quieter. The HRA financing-cost ratio has moved from 15.4% to 18.1% in a single year, driven — the paper says — by more capital borrowing and lower-than-forecast dwelling rents. Since HRA sits at 77% of your CFR, the trajectory of that ratio is really the story of the book. We can't add to what the paper says about rents; we can only price where the incremental HRA borrowing would sit on the certainty curve today.

Which is why I'd point you to the monthly sector data at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — you can see whether the market is thinning or reopening before you roll, not after — and to the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard which takes ten seconds to check.

None of it needs a meeting or a subscription. On training, three look most relevant: Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the 2012 tranche starting to roll; Interest rate risk, for the book's short-to-medium bias; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
